Kutch Ajrakh, read closely

One cloth, four chemistries

Traditional ajrakh uses four colours, blue, black, red and white, and a piece needs all four to be called ajrakh.

  • →

    Bluevadali, neela

    Indigo, then air

    Cloth lifted from the indigo vat is bright green at first and turns blue as oxygen meets the dye on the fibres.

  • →

    Blackkalo

    Iron on tannin

    On harde-treated cloth kut turns a deep, fast chocolate-black as the iron in the paste oxidises with the tannic acid.

  • →

    Redlaal

    Madder on alum

    The long thin roots of Indian madder, Rubia cordifolia or majeeta, give a dye that binds to the alum mordant and develops red where pa and gach were printed.

  • or

    Whitesafed, dhodo

    Lime keeps it

    Lime in the outline resist discharges alum, so the pa paste must not touch khariyanu areas or no red will develop in the later dyeing. Natural madder roots hold more complex colour compounds than synthetic alizarin, so madder dyeing often leaves a pinkish tinge on the white areas.

In Karolia and Buch, vadali or neela is blue, the sky; laal is red, the light of sunset; safed or dhodo is white, the stars; and kalo is black, the dark night.

Sources differ on what the colours mean
The GI application reads ajrakh's palette as the universe, with red for the earth, black for darkness, white for clouds and blue for the universe.

3Kutch Ajrakh, the monograph opening

MonographTextiles · Hand block printing

Kutch Ajrakh

Registered geographical indication, 22 April 2024Kachchh, Gujarat

Drawn from 20 sourcesA 9B 7C 4Curated 17 Nov 2026

The monograph

Kutch Ajrakh is an elaborate resist block-printing technique of direct and resist printing and dyeing, made by Khatri artisans as a double-sided textile. Its tradition is kept up in the Kutch villages of Ajrakhpur, Dhamadka and Khavda, and its process and designs are common to Sindh, where it originated, and to Barmer district of Rajasthan. A traditional piece needs all four colours, blue, black, red and white, and the most highly prized cloths were printed identically on both sides.

  • 3Ajrakh: Rhythm of Blues
  • 5GI Journal No. 188: Kutch Ajrakh, 2023
  • 6Ajrakh: From Caste Dress to Catwalk, 2016
  • 7AJRAKH- A Textile Tradition in Transition, 2016
  • 8Ajarkh, the resist printed fabric of Gujarat, 2008
  • 9Indigo in Kutch, India, 2024

1

1

At a glance

Centres
Ajrakhpur, Dhamadka and Khavda in Kachchh; also Barmer and Sindh
Makers and wearers
Khatri printers; worn as caste dress by Maldhari cattle herders
Colours
Blue, black, red and white
Dyes and mordants
Indigo, madder or alizarin, iron black on myrobalan, alum
Stages
14 to 16, depending on the source
Time per piece
About 15 to 21 days
Resists
Lime and gum outlines; clay, millet flour and alum gach
One side or both
Ek-puri on one side, bi-puri on both; identical bi-puri the most prized

In the record

  1. Mohenjo-daro

    Block printers identify the trefoil on the shawl of the Mohenjo-daro priest-king bust with kakar, the cloud motif of ajrakh.

  2. 11th to 14th century

    In 1930 hundreds of Indian cotton fragments of the 11th to 14th century were found at Al Fustat in Old Cairo, the earliest known printed cloth. The Fustat fragments, simple patterns printed with small blocks and resist dyed in indigo and madder, bear a striking similarity to ajrak.

  3. 1586 to 1631

    Rao Bharmalji I of Kutch, who ruled from 1586 to 1631, invited Khatri cloth printers from Sindh and gave them land and freedom from tax.

  4. About 1855 to 1879

    The V&A holds pieces of an ajrakh of block-printed cotton made in Sind around 1855 to 1879 and transferred from the India Museum in 1879.

  5. 2006

    A 2006 ajrakh shawl in the V&A has repeating red, white and black star-like patterns on indigo, made of two 90 cm panels sewn together. A 2006 ajrakh turban cloth by Ismail Mohammad Khatri in the V&A carries the cloud design called kakar.

2

2

How it is made

Sources count 14, 15 to 16 or 16 stages, and the GI journal gives approximately 15 to 21 days for the whole process.

  • 5GI Journal No. 188: Kutch Ajrakh, 2023
  • 8Ajarkh, the resist printed fabric of Gujarat, 2008
  • 12Traditional Indian textile designs for new markets (MA thesis), 2012
  • 13Water woes: Kutch's age-old Ajrakh craft, 2019

  1. 1

    saajScouring

    Washes and beats the cloth; traditionally it was soaked in soda ash and castor oil, then camel dung, to soften it.

    The GI journal says the soaking and drying is repeated eight to ten times, leaving the cloth bright white and soft.

    Sources differ on how many times
    Clifford records 7 to 9 rounds, until the cloth foams when rubbed.

    Cloth afterbright white and soft

    Castor oil (Ricinus communis) · Soda ash · Camel dung

  2. 2

    kasanuMyrobalan

    Soaks the cloth in harda, myrobalan, pounds it with the feet, dries it and beats off the extra powder.

    The tannin in myrobalan is a pre-mordant that helps the later printed mordants hold on the cotton.

    Cloth afterpale yellow

    Myrobalan (harda) (Terminalia chebula)

  3. 3

    rekhOutline resist

    Also called khariyanu, prints the white outlines with a carved block and a resist paste of lime and gum, usually in the morning.

    For double-sided ajrakh the outline is printed again on the reverse, matched by small registration marks on the block corners.

    Cloth afterwhite outlines in lime resist

    Lime · Gum arabic (babul gum) (Acacia nilotica)

  4. 4

    Drying

    Dries the outline-printed cloth in the sun, turning it over to dry the other side when both faces will be printed.

    Cloth afterdry on both faces

  5. 5

    katIron black

    Prints black with a paste once made of gum, ferrous sulphate and fuller’s earth, now of scrap iron, tamarind seed powder and jaggery.

    Sources differ on the paste
    The GI journal describes kut as jaggery in which scrap iron and gram flour have fermented for ten to fifteen days; Clifford gives about a week in the hot season and two in the cold.

    Cloth afterchocolate-black where printed

    Scrap iron · Jaggery · Tamarind seed powder (Tamarindus indica) · Ferrous sulphate · Fuller's earth · Gram flour

  6. 6

    paAlum mordant

    Stamps small star-like areas with tamarind seed powder boiled in alum, tinted with a fugitive dye, kesari rang.

    Cloth afterkesari-tinted stars of alum

    Alum · Tamarind seed powder (Tamarindus indica)

  7. 7

    gachMud resist

    Stamps a khor resist of alum, gum arabic, millet flour and red clay, then a resist of lime and gum arabic.

    The clay and millet flour resist indigo, while the alum is a mordant for the red to come.

    Cloth afterclay over the parts that must stay out of the blue

    Alum · Gum arabic (babul gum) (Acacia nilotica) · Millet flour · Clay · Lime

  8. 8

    Indigo

    Dyes the cloth in indigo for 10 to 15 minutes, traditionally in a naand dug into the ground.

    Cloth lifted from the vat is bright green at first and turns blue as oxygen meets the dye on the fibres.

    Cloth aftergreen, then blue in the air

    Indigo (Indigofera tinctoria) · Casatoria seeds · Sodium hydrosulphite (hydros) · Caustic soda · Sajikhar salt

  9. 9

    vichharnuWashing

    Washes the cloth in running water without hard rubbing, so the khor resist stays and the cloth remains stiff.

    Cloth afterstiff, the khor resist kept

  10. 10

    rangRed

    Boils the cloth for 2 to 3 hours with tamarisk galls and madder, then washes and sun-dries it.

    Sources differ on the order
    In the GI journal the red dyeing comes straight after the alum printing, before the gach and the indigo.

    Cloth afterred where alum was printed

    Madder (Rubia cordifolia) · Tamarisk galls · Alizarin · Al root

  11. 11

    minakariSecond round

    Repeats stages 7 to 10 once more, to give brighter and more brilliant shades of red and blue.

    Clifford calls this second round minakari, a Persian word for enamelling used in Kachchh for double work.

    Cloth afterbrighter red and blue

    Alum

Then6 pa · 7 gach · 8 indigo · 9 vichharnu · 10 rang · 11 minakari

The chemistry

Water rich in alum, tin or chrome deposits brightens ajrakh colours, while iron in the water supply dulls and darkens the result.

  • 5GI Journal No. 188: Kutch Ajrakh, 2023

Chapter 4

Why Kachchh

Ajrakh is also described as a water-intensive 16-stage process, with one step done each day before the cloth is rested.

The Great Rann of Kachchh: salt flat, not sea. Photo: Ranjith Kumar Inbasekaran, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

For 450 years

For 450 years

The GI application states that ajrakh work went on at Dhamadka for the past 450 years because a stream of the Indus gave it water. Unlike other Kachchh rivers, which rose in the Banni grasslands and flowed south, the Dhamadka river flowed the opposite way and emptied into the Banni.

Late 1980s

Late 1980s

Edwards writes that the River Suran served Dhamadka until the late 1980s, when a dam built upstream at Tapper village stopped its flow.

    1989

    1989

    The water stream at Dhamadka dried up in 1989, and water levels in its wells and tanks continued to fall.

      2001

      2001

      In 2001 an earthquake that caused severe damage in Kutch almost destroyed Dhamadka, which lay only 20 km from the epicentre. After the 2001 earthquake Dhamadka's water held a greater concentration of iron, which saddens dye colours and makes printed designs appear dull.

        After 2001

        After 2001

        After the 2001 earthquake the block printers of Dhamadka moved 40 km away, in search of good quality groundwater, to a new village named Ajrakhpur. Ajrakhpur, developed after the 2001 earthquake for the printers of Dhamadka with Gujarat government support, lies 12 km from Bhuj.

          Now

          Now

          At Ajrakhpur water once rose at a depth of 200 feet, but an artisan's later private borewell had to reach 450 feet. Excess iron, a dwindling water table and rising salinity in groundwater now threaten the craft at Ajrakhpur, as iron once did at Dhamadka.

            The season

            The season

            With the onset of the monsoon all block-printing production stops, as humidity affects the dyes and many procedures are carried out in the open.

              How does indigo turn blue on Kutch Ajrakh cloth?

              Cloth lifted from the indigo vat is bright green at first and turns blue as oxygen meets the dye on the fibres. Indigo is insoluble in water, so the vat reduces it to a soluble leuco form, leucoindigo, which enters the fibre and oxidises back to insoluble blue in the air. A traditional vat does the reducing by fermentation, with naturally occurring microbes; today ajrakh’s synthetic indigo is set in a clay maat with sodium hydrosulphite and caustic soda.

              Inside the vat

              Ajrakh indigo is either natural indigo from the plant Indigofera tinctoria or a synthesised substitute known as German indigo. Indigofera tinctoria, once cultivated on a vast commercial scale in India, is now confined to a few areas, chiefly around Tindivanam in Tamil Nadu.

              Clifford records a natural indigo vat of indigo, sagikhar salt, lime, casiatora seed and water, fermented for about one month, sometimes with jaggery.

              Sources differ: months, or about one month
              Karolia and Buch leave indigo and casatoria seeds in the naand for months. Clifford records about one month.

              Synthetic indigo is set in a clay maat with sodium hydrosulphite and caustic soda and is left to mature for 3 to 4 days. Elsewhere, chemical reduction with sodium dithionite has replaced fermentation, and its products make dye waste hard to dispose of.

              جواب7 ماخذوں سےA 4B 2C 1کچھ اجرک مونوگراف17 نومبر 2026 کو مرتب

              کچھ اجرک کے کپڑے پر نیل کیسے نیلا ہوتا ہے؟

              نیل کی ناند سے نکالا گیا کپڑا پہلے چمکدار سبز ہوتا ہے، اور جوں جوں ریشوں پر لگے رنگ سے آکسیجن ملتی ہے، وہ نیلا ہوتا جاتا ہے۔ نیل پانی میں حل نہیں ہوتا، اس لیے ناند اسے ایک حل پذیر بے رنگ شکل، لیوکو انڈیگو، میں بدل دیتی ہے جو ریشے میں سما جاتی ہے اور ہوا میں پھر سے ناحل پذیر نیلا رنگ بن جاتی ہے۔ روایتی ناند میں یہ کام خمیر کرتا ہے، جسے قدرتی طور پر موجود جرثومے انجام دیتے ہیں؛ آج اجرک کا مصنوعی نیل مٹی کے مات میں سوڈیم ہائیڈروسلفائٹ اور کاسٹک سوڈا کے ساتھ تیار کیا جاتا ہے۔
